A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LogSumExp/safe-KL research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison. The relocated kernel experiment and retained figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on Gaussian optimal transport, California-housing KL-DRO, and noisy-label MNIST, including convergence curves and repeated-run summaries.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and reports additional neural optimal-transport experiments and expanded California-housing comparisons.

M1.justification: The general SoftPlus approximation remains unchanged, but the eOT application receives a substantive adaptation. Equations (14)–(15) replace v1's scalar auxiliary variable α with a function α(x); v2 learns both potentials using neural networks. Appendix B.2 retains the original scalar-α kernel procedure as a restricted implementation.

E1.justification: V2 adds image-domain transport between MNIST digits and EMNIST letters using Manhattan cost, substantially extending coverage beyond v1's one-dimensional Gaussian transport. This is a new use of MNIST, distinct from the retained noisy-label classification task. Gaussian transport and California-housing regression remain covered.

E2.justification: V2 adds LSOT (Seguy et al., 2018) as the evaluated neural-eOT comparator in Figure 2. Genevay et al. (2016) remains in the relocated kernel experiment. California housing retains the Levy et al. (2020) baseline, and noisy MNIST retains ERM and the Wang et al. (2024) approach. Other newly discussed OT solvers are not evaluated.

E3.justification: The new neural-eOT experiment introduces batch size 256, dedicated-test-set semi-dual evaluation, and regularization comparisons at ε = 1, 10^-2, and 10^-4. California housing expands λ from 1 to {1/5, 1, 5}, changes the tested ρ values from {10^-4, 10^-3, 10^-2} to {10^-1, 10^-3, 10^-5}, and extends the learning-rate grid down to 10^-9. These are reported protocol changes, rather than newly disclosed unchanged settings.

E4.justification: V2 extends the existing kernel-stability and batch-size analyses with neural-eOT sensitivity to ε and ρ, including explicit overflow examples. Table 1 also examines California-housing performance across λ, batch size, and ρ, providing substantially broader evidence about approximation accuracy and optimization sensitivity than v1's selected-configuration curves.

E5.justification: California-housing summaries change from 20 runs in v1 Figure 3 to 10 runs in v2 Table 1. The new neural-eOT figure reports five runs. Mean and standard-deviation reporting remains the practice; the retained kernel and noisy-MNIST experiments preserve their run counts and the disclosed exclusion of one failed MNIST baseline run.

E6.justification: V2 adds neural-eOT results showing LSOT stagnation or overflow under weak regularization while the proposed approach progresses. Table 1 replaces the California convergence curves with expanded endpoint results, including a baseline advantage at λ = 1/5 and batch size 1000: 9.1 ± 4.6 versus the best proposed value of 24.3 ± 0.3. These are new or revised-setting results, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1. Kernel and noisy-MNIST results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds an explicit proof of Lemma 2.7, deriving fρ''(t) = 1/[t(1−ρt)] ≥ 4ρ and establishing the stated strong-convexity and conjugate-smoothness properties. V2 also revises the eOT auxiliary-variable domain and corrects the Gibbs extremum wording from minimum to maximum. The principal approximation bounds, CVaR results, and Appendix C proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, enumerated contributions, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: a tunable safe-KL/SoftPlus approximation, preserved convexity and smoothness, stochastic optimization benefits, and empirical advantages in OT and DRO. The additional evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds practical interpretations of the tradeoff between large-ρ approximation error and small-ρ optimization difficulty, and explicitly qualifies scalar α as an empirical restriction of the kernel experiment. It extends the California performance interpretation across λ values, although its assertion of comparable large-batch performance does not consistently match Table 1.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new neural-eOT implementation with hidden-layer widths 256 and 128, ReLU activations, batch size, learning-rate search, cost function, and test-set evaluation. It also clarifies the retained kernel experiment's shared scalar α. The code-access information and detailed kernel/MNIST implementation descriptions remain available.

R1.justification: Related-work coverage expands substantially to unbiased estimators, partition-function estimation, deterministic LogSumExp optimization, and numerical stabilization. New Appendix B.1 reviews neural, energy-based, and Schrödinger-bridge OT approaches, while Section 3.1 positions LSOT through computational expense and support for general costs. This materially broadens the paper's research positioning.

P1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix B are substantially reorganized: neural eOT becomes the main example, while the former main-text kernel study is integrated with its appendix derivations. Section 3.2 is rewritten around parameter comparisons rather than convergence trajectories. The introduction and related-work explanations expand, while the main theoretical narrative remains largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds a three-panel neural-eOT figure and replaces v1's three-panel California convergence figure with a grouped numerical table. The former main-text kernel figure moves to Appendix B as Figure 5. The safe-KL illustration, Gaussian densities, and noisy-MNIST plots reuse unchanged image content despite relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation beyond v1's Gaussian eOT and single-λ regression setup, clarifies the functional eOT auxiliary variable, and supplies an explicit proof of Lemma 2.7. These improve substantiation and clarity. The gain is tempered by replacing California learning trajectories with endpoints and by overstating large-batch comparability despite Table 1's clear baseline advantage at λ = 1/5 and batch size 1000. The net quality improvement is therefore limited.
